clue.text: Ambiguous, like the joint winners of a song contest?

definitions.text: like the joint winners of a song contest?

explanation.surface: A song contest ends in a tie, and the verdict is murky.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the word as EQUI-VOCAL: equal voices, as two singers sharing first prize would have.
explanation.definitionFit: Equivocal language can be read two ways; read as equal plus vocal it describes singers judged level.

clue.text: Urged — by missiles to leave the platform ?

definitions.text: by missiles to leave the platform

explanation.surface: A speaker is hurried off stage under a hail of thrown objects.
explanation.walkthrough: To egg on is to urge; a speaker pelted with eggs has been egged in the literal sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Egging someone on is spurring or encouraging them; an unpopular orator may also be pelted with eggs.

clue.text: The love that loves a scarlet coat Should be more (Hood)

definitions.text: The love that loves a scarlet coat Should be more (Hood)

parts.words: The love that loves a scarlet coat Should be more (Hood)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Thomas Hood: the missing word ends the line about loving a soldier's red coat

explanation.surface: A line of verse by Thomas Hood with its final word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan shows a dash after 'more' for the missing word; Hood's couplet puns on the word as 'more consistent' and as a soldier's dress.
explanation.definitionFit: A scarlet coat is military dress, and the poet wants love to be more constant, playing on regimental dress and sameness.

clue.text: Viz., in full

parts.note: asks for the full Latin word that the short form viz. stands for

explanation.definitionFit: Viz. is the abbreviation of the Latin word meaning namely or that is to say.

clue.text: A statement given with some qualification?

definitions.text: A statement given with some qualification?

parts.words: A statement given with some qualification?
parts.note: a qualification sounds like a hedge on a statement, but it is an exam pass, and the document stating it is handed over

explanation.surface: A guarded remark offered with reservations.
explanation.definitionFit: A diploma or official document states that the holder has gained a qualification.

clue.text: Where there's no smoke without fire in Scotland

definitions.text: Where there's no smoke without fire in Scotland

parts.words: Where there's no smoke without fire in Scotland
parts.note: the proverb points to the place smoke rises from a hearth, named with a Scots word

explanation.surface: A twist on the proverb that rumours always have some basis.
explanation.walkthrough: LUM is the Scots word for a chimney, where smoke from the fire goes up.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots dialect a lum is a chimney, the flue a household fire sends its smoke up.

clue.text: French author brings 14 ac to us

parts.note: the answer to 14 across, a shaft
taken as written

explanation.surface: A French writer is said to bring something to the reader.
explanation.walkthrough: 14 across is CAM, a rotating shaft; Albert Camus wrote The Outsider.
explanation.definitionFit: Albert Camus was a French novelist and philosopher, author of The Plague.

clue.text: In receipt of optimum clue-number

parts.note: this clue is number six, and receiving six of the best is a schoolboy beating

explanation.surface: Someone is awarded the best clue number.
explanation.walkthrough: Optimum means best and this clue's number is 6: 'six of the best' is a caning with six strokes.
explanation.definitionFit: Six of the best was the traditional British school punishment of six strokes with a rod.

clue.text: A disorderly Vale mob can be shifted

indicators.note: a disorderly crowd is in disarray, so these letters are to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An unruly crowd from the valley can be moved on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disorderly' rearranges VALE MOB; the opening 'A' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something portable is able to be moved or shifted from place to place.

clue.text: Yield more certain round the right extremity

indicators.note: the comparative word goes round the other pieces, enclosing them

parts.note: surer means more certain
an end is an extremity

explanation.surface: A command to give way more surely at the far right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' puts R plus END inside SURER, after SUR; 'the' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To yield is to give in or hand over, as an army capitulating.

clue.text: Would this money improve Lily, would you say?

indicators.note: spoken words signal that the answer is a word that sounds like another

parts.note: to gild the lily is to try to improve what is already perfect, so one who does it is a gilder

explanation.surface: A question whether cash could make Lily more attractive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lily' looks like a name; it is the flower in 'gild the lily'. The Dutch coin sounds like one who gilds.
explanation.definitionFit: The guilder was the currency unit of the Netherlands before the euro.

clue.text: Short length, nothing left over, of the white fur

parts.note: a mini is a short length, as of a skirt

indicators.note: left means gone away, so the letter for nothing departs from the word over

parts.note: taken as written
O is the zero shape, nothing

explanation.surface: A short piece of white fur, with nothing remaining.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nothing left' removes O from OVER, leaving VER.
explanation.definitionFit: Miniver is a white fur used to trim ceremonial robes, such as peers' robes.

clue.text: Peer sent back money-funny!

indicators.note: something sent back goes the other way, so the word is read in reverse

parts.note: a lord is a peer of the realm
L stands for pound (libra), money

explanation.surface: An aristocrat returns cash, which is amusing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sent back' reverses LORD to DROL; L is the pound sign's letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Droll means amusing in a dry or odd way.

clue.text: Bail in due form — unheard of ?

indicators.note: to form something is to shape it anew, so these letters are put together in a fresh order

explanation.surface: Granting bail in the proper manner is unprecedented.
explanation.walkthrough: 'form' rearranges BAIL IN DUE; 'of' is a link and 'unheard of' tempts as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something too quiet to catch is not heard at all.

clue.text: Admit to an understanding of electricity ?

parts.note: AC, alternating current, is electricity
knowledge is an understanding of a subject

explanation.surface: To confess to knowing about electricity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'an understanding of electricity' read literally is knowledge of AC, written AC first.
explanation.definitionFit: To acknowledge is to concede or own up to something.

clue.text: About a thousand in this shaft

parts.note: ca is the short form of circa, about
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

explanation.surface: Around a thousand people are in this mine shaft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in this' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A cam is a rotating projection on a shaft in machinery, the camshaft.

clue.text: Topping way one contends with a way of speaking

parts.note: copes with means contends with
tone is a manner of speaking

explanation.surface: The best way to deal with an awkward manner of speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topping' sounds like 'excellent', but it is the top course of a wall.
explanation.definitionFit: A copestone is the stone laid on top of a wall or building, its crowning topping.

clue.text: Small change at the Coop ?

explanation.surface: Spare coins handed over at the Co-op shop.
explanation.walkthrough: The Co-op is a British shop; a coop houses hens, where chicken feed is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: A trivial sum of money is slang for a paltry amount; literally it is grain for hens.

clue.text: Exemplified by Browning's Home-thoughts from Abroad "

definitions.text: Exemplified by Browning's Home-thoughts from Abroad "

parts.words: Exemplified by Browning's Home-thoughts from Abroad "
parts.note: Browning's poem 'Oh, to be in England' expresses an exile's longing for home

explanation.surface: A remark about a famous Browning poem.
explanation.walkthrough: The poem opens 'Oh, to be in England / Now that April's there', written while abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: A wistful yearning for home or the past is what Browning's poem voices.

clue.text: Cheap betrayers, we hear, force their way in

indicators.note: says the answer is a word sounding like the phrase

parts.note: a penny is cheap and traitors are betrayers

explanation.surface: Low-grade traitors forcing an entry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penny traitors' said quickly sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who penetrate break into or pierce a place.

clue.text: Next-of-kin, Eastern variety

indicators.note: a variety of something is a different form, so the letters take another order

explanation.surface: A relative of oriental kind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'variety' rearranges EASTERN.
explanation.definitionFit: Your closest relative is the one nearest in kinship, the next of kin.

clue.text: Local pressure unit ?

explanation.surface: A question about a small unit of pressure.
explanation.walkthrough: A local is a British pub, the one near your home; the bar is also a unit of pressure.
explanation.definitionFit: A bar is a pub, the local; it is also a metric unit of atmospheric pressure.

clue.text: Post for which the management are about fifty-fifty

indicators.note: about means around, so the board surrounds the fifties

parts.note: a board of directors is the management
L is the Roman numeral for fifty, given twice

explanation.surface: A post on which the bosses split the difference.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fifty-fifty' looks like an equal split but gives two Ls; 'for which' and 'are' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A bollard is a short thick post for mooring ships or blocking traffic.

clue.text: Chief player's ordeal by fire highlights the scene .

parts.note: the star is the chief player, with the possessive giving S
hell is a fiery torment

explanation.surface: A lead actor's trial by fire as the stage lights go up.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots carry on to 22 across, which describes the lit scene.
explanation.definitionFit: A star shell is a flare fired to light up a battlefield at night.

clue.text: Ship coming home when a weekly gamble comes up?

indicators.note: in a down clue coming up means read from bottom to top

parts.note: the pools is the British weekly football betting coupon

explanation.surface: One's ship comes in when a pools win comes up.
explanation.walkthrough: The football pools was a British weekly betting game; 'ship coming home' evokes a win.
explanation.definitionFit: A sloop is a one-masted sailing ship.

clue.text: so it's this, through a shortage of silver

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
being low is having a shortage

explanation.surface: The scene is glowing because silver is running short.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue continues 20 across: the scene a star shell lights up is this. 'a shortage of silver' gives silver low, AG then LOW.
explanation.definitionFit: A scene lit by flares is glowing, bright with light.

clue.text: Hamelin's wall-washer

parts.note: Browning's Pied Piper says the river 'washes its wall on the southern side' of Hamelin

explanation.surface: Someone who cleans the town walls of Hamelin.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamelin is the Pied Piper town on the river Weser.
explanation.definitionFit: The Weser is the German river flowing past Hamelin's walls.

clue.text: Oppressive one confuses ours

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: confusing letters jumbles them into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone oppressive mixes up what belongs to us.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confuses' rearranges OURS to ROUS, placed after ONE.
explanation.definitionFit: Burdensome tasks weigh on you, being heavy and oppressive.

clue.text: Resort would be within a foreign country

definitions.text: Resort would be within a foreign country

parts.words: Resort would be within a foreign country
parts.note: a holiday resort followed by the word within names a European country

explanation.surface: A holiday resort lies inside a foreign land.
explanation.walkthrough: The resort word plus IN spells SPAIN, so the resort 'would be within' Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: A spa is a resort with mineral springs.

clue.text: They're hot, maybe dodgy as summer-time can be

indicators.note: maybe suggests the letters could be arranged otherwise

explanation.surface: Hot days can be shady, as summer often is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' rearranges DODGY AS; 'as summer-time can be' extends the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The sultry period of high summer, named after the Dog Star, is the hottest part of the year.

clue.text: 19 ac only partly goes to press

indicators.note: only partly says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A partial printing of the newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft's definition 'ac' is only part of the cross-reference: the definition is '19 ac', BAR.
explanation.definitionFit: To estop is a legal word meaning to bar or prevent someone.

clue.text: The Great Band-leader

explanation.surface: A great bandleader.
explanation.walkthrough: Alexander the Great, and Irving Berlin's song 'Alexander's Ragtime Band'.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexander the Great was the Macedonian conqueror; the band leader is the one in Alexander's Ragtime Band.
